rows.name: The Lamplighters' Tide
rows.concept: A fog-wrapped harbor town where lamplighters trade in half-remembered names and the tide carries old debts ashore.
rows.tone: melancholic gothic mystery with a slow, salt-soaked dread — quiet, intimate, and haunted rather than overtly horrific
rows.themes: The weight of forgotten names and unpaid debts. Memory as currency and as curse. The sea as keeper of secrets it always, eventually, returns. The fragile rituals that hold a community together against the dark.
rows.geography_summary: A cramped harbor town built on rotting piers and fog-slicked cobblestones, hemmed in by black cliffs and a tidal estuary that swallows the lower streets twice a day. Beyond the breakwater, a cold grey sea exhales mist that never fully lifts, and the inland moors climb into pine and standing stones.
rows.political_summary: Nominal authority rests with a harbormaster's council and an old merchant guild, but real power lies with the Lamplighters' Guild, who tend the night-lanterns and broker the trade in half-remembered names. Outside debt-collectors, a distant crown's tax-writ, and something older beneath the waves all press on the town's brittle equilibrium.
rows.era: Late guttering-medieval with early gaslight and clockwork — black-powder pistols exist but are rare, ledgers and lantern-oil matter more than steel
rows.key_tensions: The Lamplighters' monopoly on names is fraying: someone has begun selling true-names to outsiders, and the Guild knows but cannot prove who. The tide has lately begun returning things it should not — corpses too well-preserved, sea-chests sealed with sigils no one living recognizes, a child who walked out of the surf speaking a dead dialect. A crown auditor has arrived to collect three generations of unpaid harbor levies, and the town's books are full of debts owed to people who no longer exist, or never did. Beneath it all, the lighthouse keeper has stopped lighting the outer lamp, and no one will say why.
rows.world_overview: The town of Coldhaven huddles where the Tyne estuary meets a cold grey sea, three centuries of harbor levies in arrears and the outer lamp of its lighthouse gone dark for the first time in living memory. The town is a vertical thing: the Upper Town clings to the bluff under the lighthouse, the Pier District works the middle wharves where the Lamplighters' Guild keeps its hall and the Harbormaster's Council its chambers, and the Underpiers rots and floods on stilts below, half-drowned twice a day by the Estuary Hours. Inland, the Whistlepine Moors stretch toward standing stones the Moors Compact obliges their tenders to maintain. Out past the breakwater, the open grey of the Drowning Reach hides whatever the sea is currently giving back. The Lamplighters' Guild brokers names through the Naming Trade and holds nearly every household on lantern-debt, but the Harbormaster's Council nominally governs, the Underpiers keep their own salt-ledgers in defiance, the Moor-folk answer to neither, and a crown auditor has arrived with writs that could in theory undo all of it. The Returning has been accelerating, and something quieter — the keepers of the outer lamp, the children speaking dead dialect — is moving underneath the politics in a current no one quite acknowledges.
rows.follow_up_questions: Is the supernatural element overt and known to townsfolk, or a creeping suspicion most still deny? How literal is the trade in names — folk-magic ritual, true arcane binding, or shorthand for blackmail and identity-laundering? Is this town isolated and self-contained, or one node in a larger coastal polity the players can travel beyond?

entries.definition: The dominant power in the harbor town, ostensibly a trade guild responsible for maintaining, fueling, and lighting the town's network of night-lanterns. In practice, the Guild serves as brokers, custodians, and enforcers of the trade in half-remembered names. Membership is hereditary or by invitation, and Guild members are recognizable by their brass-capped oil-canisters and the faint smell of rendered tallow that clings to their coats. Their authority is informal but absolute — a shopkeeper who offends the Guild may find their lantern unlit for a season.
entries.usage_notes: Always capitalized. Referred to as 'the Guild' in shorthand. Never called a 'union' or 'company' — those are outsider words and mark the speaker as foreign.

entries.definition: The Guild's most lucrative and most dangerous business: the brokering of half-remembered names. A name in this world carries residual weight — the more people who have forgotten a name, the more power accrues to whoever holds it intact. The Guild collects names the dying surrender, names the grieving let slip, names erased from ledgers, and trades them as currency, collateral, or weapons. A name sold through the Naming Trade cannot be spoken aloud by its former holder without cost.
entries.usage_notes: Always capitalized. Spoken of obliquely in polite company — 'the Trade' is the preferred shorthand. Outsiders who ask too directly are told it is a 'record-keeping service.'

entries.definition: A name that has begun to fade from collective memory — still known by some, but no longer anchored by daily use, written record, or living relationship. Half-remembered names are the raw material of the Naming Trade. They carry a peculiar resonance: speaking one aloud in the fog sometimes draws an answering sound from the water. The more forgotten a name becomes, the heavier and stranger it grows, until it crosses into a true-name or dissolves entirely into the tide.
entries.usage_notes: Lowercase. The hyphen is conventional and should be preserved. Do not abbreviate to 'half-name' — that means something different and insulting.

entries.definition: A name that has been completely forgotten by all living persons except the one who holds it in trust. True-names are the Guild's most valuable commodity and most closely guarded secret. Possession of a person's true-name grants leverage over them that defies easy explanation — it is not magic in the showy sense, but those who have had their true-name sold report a persistent sense of being watched, of words sticking in their throats, of dreams that belong to someone else.
entries.usage_notes: Always hyphenated, always lowercase. The Guild uses the formal term 'a sealed name' in written contracts to avoid the word appearing in documents that might be subpoenaed.

entries.definition: The folk understanding that the sea is a creditor that never forgives — anything lost to the water is merely held in escrow, and the sea will return it when the interest has compounded sufficiently. Tide Debts are spoken of as though they are legal instruments: 'the sea holds a Tide Debt on the Morrow family' means that something of theirs went into the water and has not yet come back. The recent returns of preserved corpses and sealed chests are widely interpreted as the sea collecting on very old Tide Debts.
entries.usage_notes: Capitalized as a proper concept. 'Tide debt' (lowercase) is the casual, dismissive form used by skeptics and outsiders. The distinction matters to locals.

entries.definition: The phenomenon of objects, persons, or things lost to the sea coming back — washed ashore, walking out of the surf, or found in sealed rooms that were locked from the inside. The Returning is not new, but its recent acceleration has the town frightened. Things that Return are not always what they were: the well-preserved corpses smell of deep brine rather than rot, the sealed chests open to reveal documents in hands no notary recognizes, and the child who walked out of the surf has not aged but speaks in a dialect three centuries dead.
entries.usage_notes: Always capitalized when referring to the current phenomenon. 'A returning' (lowercase, indefinite article) refers to a single instance of something coming back.

entries.definition: A social and quasi-legal obligation created when the Guild lights a lantern for a household or business that cannot pay its oil-tithe. The Guild records the debt in its ledgers, and until it is settled, the debtor's name is held as soft collateral — not yet sold, but flagged. A household carrying lantern-debt is said to be 'burning on credit.' Lantern-debts are heritable and can accumulate across generations, which is how the Guild has come to hold leverage over nearly every family in town.
entries.usage_notes: Lowercase, hyphenated. 'On lantern-debt' is the prepositional phrase. Do not confuse with Tide Debt — lantern-debt is a Guild instrument; Tide Debt is a cosmological one.

entries.definition: The Guild's master record of names that have passed through the Naming Trade — who surrendered them, who purchased them, and at what price. The Ledger is a physical object: a water-stained folio bound in grey leather, kept in the Guild's inner sanctum. It is also, in a secondary sense, the town's collective memory of everyone who has been forgotten, which gives it a weight that unnerves even senior Guild members. Pages have been known to add themselves overnight.
entries.usage_notes: Always capitalized. Referred to as 'the Ledger' in Guild speech. Outsiders who ask to see it are told it is 'under audit' — a lie that has been in continuous use for forty years.

entries.definition: The regular payment — in coin, labor, or name-credit — that households and businesses owe the Guild in exchange for their lanterns being lit. The oil-tithe is collected monthly by the Guild's junior members, called wicktenders. Failure to pay converts the tithe to a lantern-debt. The oil-tithe is the Guild's public-facing revenue stream and the mechanism by which it maintains surveillance over who is home, who is absent, and who has stopped answering the door.
entries.usage_notes: Lowercase, hyphenated. 'Tithe' alone is acceptable in context. Do not use 'tax' — the Guild is extremely sensitive about this distinction, especially with the crown auditor in town.

entries.definition: A junior member of the Lamplighters' Guild, responsible for collecting oil-tithes, trimming wicks, refilling reservoirs, and reporting irregularities to senior lamplighters. Wicktenders are the Guild's eyes on the street — they know which households are behind on payments, which doors go unanswered, which windows show light at hours when no one should be awake. Most are young, most are local, and most have been in the Guild's orbit since childhood.
entries.usage_notes: Lowercase. Plural: wicktenders. Not a term of contempt, but wicktenders who aspire to full lamplighter status are careful not to be called 'just a wicktender' by their seniors.

entries.definition: The nominal governing body of the town, composed of the harbormaster, two senior guild merchants, a representative of the clergy, and a rotating seat held by whichever fishing cooperative is currently largest. The Council issues permits, settles commercial disputes, and maintains the public fiction that the town governs itself. In practice it defers to the Lamplighters' Guild on any matter that touches on names, debts, or the night. The Council's authority is real but bounded — they can hang a man for murder but not for selling a name.
entries.usage_notes: Always capitalized. 'The Council' in shorthand. Individual members are 'Councillors.' The harbormaster herself is addressed as 'Harbormaster' — never 'Chair' or 'President.'

entries.definition: The lighthouse's seaward-facing beacon, distinct from the inner lamp that guides ships through the estuary mouth. The outer lamp is older, its mechanism poorly understood even by the current lighthouse keeper, and it has burned continuously for as long as anyone's great-grandparents can remember. Its recent extinction — quiet, unannounced, the keeper offering no explanation — is the most frightening thing to happen in the town in a generation, though most residents cannot articulate precisely why.
entries.usage_notes: Lowercase. Always 'the outer lamp,' never 'the outer light' or 'the outer beacon' — those are the terms used on nautical charts, and locals find them clinical and wrong.

entries.definition: A superstition, or possibly a practice — the habit of leaving a small offering (a coin, a pinch of salt, a written name on paper) at the waterline when the tide is going out, as payment to the fog for the visibility it occasionally grants. Older residents perform this without thinking; younger ones do it ironically and then keep doing it. The fog-tithe is not Guild-sanctioned but the Guild does not discourage it, as it reinforces the idea that the fog is an entity with whom one negotiates rather than a weather phenomenon one endures.
entries.usage_notes: Lowercase, hyphenated. Spoken of casually. Performing one is 'leaving a fog-tithe' or simply 'tithing the fog.'

entries.definition: The twice-daily period when the tidal estuary floods the lower streets, rendering the Underpiers district impassable on foot without a boat or stilts. During the Estuary Hours, business in the lower town halts, debts cannot be legally served, and — by a Guild convention that has acquired the force of law — no names may be formally transferred. The Estuary Hours are also when most of the Returning events occur, which has made the flooding feel less like a nuisance and more like a threshold.
entries.usage_notes: Always capitalized. Referred to in the plural even when discussing a single tidal event. 'During the Hours' is acceptable shorthand.

entries.definition: The lowest district of the harbor town, built on rotting wooden piers and tidal mudflats, accessible only during low water. The Underpiers house the town's poorest residents, its least-licensed fishmongers, and its most informal economies. During the Estuary Hours the district floods to waist height; its residents have adapted with raised sleeping platforms and waterproof document chests. The Underpiers are also where most things that Return first appear, which means the district's residents have developed the most elaborate protocols for dealing with them.
entries.usage_notes: Always capitalized. Singular as a place name: 'the Underpiers is flooded,' not 'the Underpiers are.' Residents call it 'the Unders' among themselves.

entries.definition: Describes objects, documents, or persons that have been in the sea and returned in an unnatural state of preservation — no rot, no waterlogging, sometimes no evidence of submersion at all except a faint smell of deep salt and cold. Brine-sealed objects are treated with extreme caution: they may be legally unclaimed (since their original owners are presumed dead), but the Guild holds that anything brine-sealed carries a Tide Debt that transfers to whoever takes possession of it.
entries.usage_notes: Hyphenated adjective. 'Brine-sealing' as a process does not exist — it is not something done to objects, only something that happens to them. Do not use as a verb.

entries.definition: Any form of speech, writing, or gesture-language that was in use in the region before the town's founding records begin — roughly three centuries ago. The child who walked out of the surf speaks in dead dialect, which the town's oldest scholar can partially parse from marginalia in pre-Guild ledgers. Dead dialect is not merely archaic; it carries a structural logic that modern speakers find disorienting, as though the grammar itself encodes assumptions about time and identity that no longer apply.
entries.usage_notes: Lowercase. A specific technical and folk term — not a generic phrase for 'old language.' Using it casually to mean any old-fashioned speech is a marker of ignorance that locals will notice.

entries.definition: The representative of the distant crown currently resident in the town, tasked with assessing and collecting three generations of unpaid harbor levies. The auditor is not a military figure but carries writs that could theoretically authorize one — a threat the town takes seriously and the Guild takes personally. The auditor's problem is that the town's books record debts owed to persons who do not exist in any crown registry, payments made to accounts with no corresponding names, and a consistent pattern of entries that seem to have been made in anticipation of events that had not yet occurred.
entries.usage_notes: Lowercase as a title unless used as a form of address ('Auditor Vane'). Locals refer to the auditor obliquely as 'the crown's man' or 'the writ-bearer' — rarely by name, as a form of low-grade social resistance.

entries.definition: An informal record kept by fishers, pier-workers, and Underpiers residents that tracks Tide Debts, brine-sealed returns, and Returning events in a parallel accounting to the Guild's Ledger of Absences. Salt-ledgers are kept in waterproof oilskin, written in pencil or grease-crayon, and passed between trusted neighbors rather than stored in any fixed location. The Guild is aware of their existence and deeply uncomfortable with them, since they represent a rival system of memory-keeping.
entries.usage_notes: Lowercase, hyphenated. A salt-ledger is always personal or communal, never institutional. 'The salt-ledger' with a definite article refers to a specific community's record; 'a salt-ledger' is the general form.

entries.definition: A set of carved stone figures mounted on the harbor breakwater, each representing a virtue or protective principle in the old pre-crown religion of the coast. The Saints are not worshipped in any formal sense but are maintained obsessively — repainted, garlanded, left offerings of rope and dried fish. The Lamplighters' Guild has quietly adopted the Saints as part of its ritual infrastructure, lighting a small lamp at each figure's base every night. The Saints are also, according to Underpiers tradition, the reason the outer lamp matters: they are oriented toward it, not toward the town.
entries.usage_notes: Always capitalized. 'The Saints' in shorthand. Individual figures have names that are local rather than crown-canonical — 'the Knot-Keeper,' 'the Hollow-Eyed,' 'the One Who Counts.'

entries.definition: The condition of a person whose name has been fully sold through the Naming Trade and who has begun to feel its absence as a physical lack — a hollow at the sternum, difficulty being seen in crowds, the sense that mirrors take a moment too long to show their face. Name-hunger is progressive and poorly understood. The Guild officially denies it exists; the Underpiers residents have a word for it and a set of folk remedies, none of which the Guild endorses.
entries.usage_notes: Lowercase, hyphenated. Not a medical diagnosis in any formal sense. 'Suffering name-hunger' or 'deep in name-hunger' are the conventional phrasings. Do not use 'name-hungry' as an adjective for a person — it sounds flippant and locals find it offensive.

entries.definition: An old agreement, predating the current Guild and Council, between the harbor town and the communities of the inland moors — the pine-cutters, standing-stone tenders, and scattered farmsteads that supply the town with timber, peat, and certain herbs used in lamp-oil formulation. The Compact guarantees moor-folk access to the harbor market and exempts them from oil-tithe. In exchange, they maintain certain stones on the moor that are said, in the compact's original language, to 'hold the fog from the high ground.' No one currently living has read the original document; the Guild claims it is in the Ledger of Absences.
entries.usage_notes: Always capitalized. Referred to as 'the Compact' in shorthand. Moor-folk call it 'the old bargain' in their own speech — a translation, not a synonym.

entries.definition: The specific grade of animal fat used in the town's lanterns — not beeswax, not whale-oil, but tallow rendered from cattle and sheep by a process the Guild guards as a trade secret. Rendered tallow burns at a particular color (a warm amber with a slight blue edge) that locals can distinguish from any other light source. This color is culturally significant: a room lit by rendered tallow is a room under Guild visibility, and its absence in a lantern is the first sign that something is wrong with a household's standing.
entries.usage_notes: Lowercase. The specific phrase 'rendered tallow' matters — 'tallow' alone is generic; 'rendered tallow' signals the Guild-specific product. The blue-edged amber color is called 'Guild-light' colloquially.

entries.definition: The period just before dawn when the fog is thickest and the night-lanterns have burned lowest — the hour when wicktenders make their final rounds and when, by long tradition, debts may be renegotiated without formal record. The soft hour is also when most name-transfers in the Naming Trade are conducted, because the Guild holds that names spoken in the soft hour carry less risk of being overheard by the sea. Whether this is true or ritual rationalization, no one is certain.
entries.usage_notes: Lowercase. Always singular and always with the definite article — 'the soft hour,' never 'a soft hour' or 'soft hours.' Using it in the plural is a grammatical error that marks the speaker as unfamiliar with local custom.

starting_situation_entries.prose: Mer Tallow is one of the few people in Coldhaven who will speak plainly to a stranger — for a price, or a favor, or just because she finds you interesting enough. Her stall sits at the mouth of the Underpiers, where the Returning happens first, and the padlocked chest behind her has salt-rings on its lid that weren't there last season.
starting_situation_entries.title: Gutting Fish at the Edge of the Returning

starting_situation_entries.prose: The outer lamp has been dark since midsummer, and the keeper, Adwen Roak, descends to town only at dawn and says nothing to anyone. A new arrival with no lantern-debt and no name on the Ledger of Absences is one of the few people she might open the iron-bound door for — and the dark lamp-housing at the top smells of something that isn't lamp-oil.
starting_situation_entries.title: The Lamp That Stopped Burning

starting_situation_entries.prose: At the burned end of the Underpiers, a shrine built from salvaged boards holds chalked names and dried fish left for something no one will name directly — and the pale-haired child who walked out of the surf here speaks in a grammar that bends time. A stranger who sits quietly at the shrine's edge long enough may be the first outsider she chooses to address.
starting_situation_entries.title: Chalk Names and Coiled Rope

rows.name: The Lighthouse Bluff and Upper Town
The Keepers of the Outer Lamp
The Inland Shrine of the Breakwater Saints

rows.content: The middle band of Coldhaven, stacked between the bluff-road and the tideline, where the working harbor does its honest and dishonest business. Cobbled lanes climb in switchbacks between chandleries, rope-walks, the customs house, and the great slate-roofed Guildhall, every street studded at intervals with iron lantern-posts that burn the warm blue-edged amber of rendered tallow from dusk until the soft hour. The district smells of tar, tallow smoke, gutted fish, and the particular cold-iron tang the fog carries off the Reach. Wicktenders move through it at dawn and dusk with their brass canisters; merchants nod to them and do not meet their eyes. The Harbormaster's Council chambers sit at the foot of Pier Three, a squat building of grey granite with a brass weathervane shaped like a gull holding a key. Above the district, the lighthouse stands on the bluff; below it, stairs and ramps descend into the Underpiers when the tide allows.

Below the working town, on rotted piling and tidal mud, the Underpiers sprawls in a dim wooden warren that the Estuary Hours floods to waist-height twice a day. Boardwalks sag between leaning tenements; sleeping platforms are slung from rafters above the high-water line; every door has a waterproof chest bolted beside it for documents and dry clothes. The light here is what filters down between the upper boards — striped, greenish at noon, gone entirely after dusk except for fish-oil lamps and the occasional outlaw tallow-burner. The Unders smells of brine, wet pine, smoked fish, and the faint chemical sweetness of the bog-grass residents weave into mats. It is the poorest district and also the most self-governed: the Guild's wicktenders do their rounds only at low tide and never alone, and most of the people who matter here keep a salt-ledger and a short knife within arm's reach. The Returning, when it happens, happens here first — corpses, chests, and once a child, all coming out of the surf at the Pier Four ruin.

Above the Pier District a chalky bluff rises to a windswept plateau where the lighthouse stands at the seaward edge, its white tower banded in three rings of black, its inner lamp still turning, its outer lamp dark since midsummer. The Upper Town spreads inland from the lighthouse along a single high street of slate-roofed merchant houses, the old chapel of the Breakwater Saints' inland shrine, and the walled garden of the Harbormaster's residence. The wind up here is constant and the fog rarely reaches above the bluff's lip, so the Upper Town has a clarity the rest of Coldhaven lacks — one can see, on most days, all the way down the coast to the standing stones. The light, though. The light is wrong now. The outer lamp's silence has done something to the quality of evenings here that residents notice without being able to name.

Inland of Coldhaven the land lifts into a high rolling moor of heather, peat-cut, and stands of black pine that whistle in the constant wind — hence the name. The Moors are sparsely settled: pine-cutters' camps, peat-diggers' huts, three farmsteads scattered along the old drove road, and the stone-tenders' cottage at the edge of the Standing Field where seventeen monoliths lean in a rough oval against the wind. The fog that smothers the harbor breaks against the moor's lower slopes and rarely climbs higher; up on the heath the light is grey but honest, and one can see weather coming for hours. Moor-folk wear undyed wool, speak with a flatter vowel than the harbor, and come down to market once a fortnight under the protections of the Moors Compact. They do not pay oil-tithe and they do not, as a rule, sleep in Coldhaven overnight.

The grey open water beyond Coldhaven's breakwater, where the estuary's brown current meets the cold deep and the fog seems to be manufactured rather than weather. The Reach is not deep by ocean standards, but its bottom is uneven — sunken rocks, an old wreck or two, and the long shallow bank called the Tallowback that boats avoid by tradition more than by chart. Fishing crews work the Reach in the morning hours and are home before dusk; no one with sense is on the Reach after the soft hour. The outer lamp used to face it. With the lamp dark, captains have begun losing their bearings in the fog at distances they used to find by feel.

The long curving granite arm that shelters Coldhaven's harbor, walked end to end in twenty minutes on a calm day and impassable in a gale. Set into its outer face at even intervals are the carved Breakwater Saints — twenty-three of them, weather-pitted, repainted every spring, garlanded with rope and dried fish. The Walk is a public space and a quasi-religious one; courting couples promenade here, children dare each other to touch the Hollow-Eyed's face, and every night a Guild wicktender lights the small brass lamp at each Saint's base. The Saints face seaward, oriented — as the Underpiers will tell you — toward where the outer lamp used to burn, not toward the town.

The dominant power in Coldhaven and the institutional spine of the Naming Trade. The Guild presents itself as a trade body responsible for lighting the town's lanterns, rendering tallow to its proprietary formulation, and maintaining the network of oil-tithes and lantern-debts that keep Coldhaven illuminated after dark. Membership is hereditary or by invitation; Guild members wear unmarked grey wool, carry brass-capped oil-canisters, and smell faintly of tallow. The Guild is led by a Guild Master — currently Master Ovin Cawl, a thin courteous man in his sixties — and a senior council of seven lamplighters who meet in the Guildhall's upper room. Beneath them, full lamplighters supervise the wicktenders who do the street work. Outsiders find the Guild oddly soft-spoken for an organization with so much leverage; insiders understand that the softness is the leverage. The Guild holds lantern-debt on nearly every household in Coldhaven and brokers names through the Trade as collateral, currency, and quiet weapon.

The nominal civic government of Coldhaven, chambered in the granite building at the foot of Pier Three. The Council comprises Harbormaster Iselt Morrow, two senior guild merchants (currently a chandler and a rope-maker), a clergy representative from the Breakwater Saints' inland shrine, and a rotating seat held by the largest fishing cooperative. The Council issues commercial permits, settles civil disputes, and maintains the fiction of self-government. In practice it defers to the Lamplighters' Guild on anything touching names, debts, or the night, which is most things in Coldhaven. Harbormaster Morrow is a competent, tired woman in her fifties who has been in the seat for eleven years and is acutely aware of the Council's limits — she can hang a man for murder but cannot prevent the Guild from selling his name first. The arrival of the crown auditor has put the Council in an uncomfortable position between an institution they fear and a crown they cannot defy.

A formal but small crown presence in Coldhaven, currently consisting of Auditor Sera Vane and three clerks lodged in the upper rooms of the customs house. Vane was dispatched to assess and collect three generations of unpaid harbor levies — a routine assignment, on paper, that has become something else entirely as she has worked through the town's books. She is a small precise woman in dark crown-cloth, in her early forties, with the manner of someone who has audited many towns and has never before encountered books like Coldhaven's. The town receives her with elaborate civility and complete obstruction. The Guild has not yet decided whether she is a problem to be bought, neutralized, or simply outlasted; the Council is hoping she finishes her work and leaves; the Underpiers are watching with interest, as anyone who frightens the Guild is at least provisionally a friend.

An informal, deliberately leaderless network of Underpiers residents, fishers, and a few sympathetic Pier District tradespeople who maintain the salt-ledgers — parallel records of Tide Debts, Returnings, and name-transfers that the Guild does not control. The Circle has no hall, no charter, and no membership roll; it operates by overlapping copies, shared phrases, and the slow trust of people who have lived next to each other on flooded boards for generations. The closest thing it has to elders are the fishmonger Mer Tallow, who keeps the oldest continuous ledger, and a retired wicktender called Joss Pell who walked away from the Guild fifteen years ago and has been quietly copying his old route's debts ever since. The Circle's goal is memory — to make sure that what the Guild forgets, or chooses to forget, is remembered somewhere the Guild cannot reach. They are not revolutionaries. They are archivists with knives.

The scattered communities of the Whistlepine Moors — pine-cutters, peat-diggers, three farmstead families, and the hereditary stone-tenders of the Standing Field — bound to Coldhaven not by allegiance but by the Moors Compact. They are independent, undyed-wool people with a flatter vowel and a habit of leaving before dusk. Their nominal spokesperson at market is whichever farmstead-elder is currently strongest, but the actual authority among them is the eldest stone-tender, currently Ifor Penny, a small grey woman of indeterminate age who has lived in the tender's cottage for as long as anyone in Coldhaven can remember. The moor-folk do not pay oil-tithe, do not engage in the Naming Trade, and do not consider themselves subject to the Guild — a position the Guild has tolerated for two centuries because the Compact is older than the Guild and the Guild does not, in fact, know what the Compact actually obliges.

Not a faction in any public sense — a hereditary trust of three families whose ancestors, three centuries ago, made an arrangement with what the moor-folk call the far-listener. The Keepers are the lighthouse line (currently Adwen Roak), a senior line within the Lamplighters' Guild (currently Master Ovin Cawl), and one family from the Breakwater Saints' inland shrine (currently Sister Onella Drake of the Council). The three are bound by sealed letters opened at the elevation of each new Keeper, and they have never met as a body in living memory — communication is by single messengers and ritual phrases. Their job, collectively, was to keep the outer lamp burning, to ensure that names entered the Ledger of Absences at a steady rate, and to maintain the standing stones' alignment with the lamp. They have failed at the third for some decades, did not realize the second was failing until recently, and Adwen Roak has now, for reasons she has not fully explained, deliberately failed the first.

A slate-roofed building of grey granite occupies the corner where Pier Three meets the switchback lanes, its facade unmarked except for a single iron lantern over the door that burns rendered tallow even at noon. The front hall is panelled in dark oak gone soft with tallow-smoke; the air smells of warm fat and old paper. A long counter divides the public chamber from the inner offices, manned by a clerk in unmarked grey wool who looks up only when addressed. Behind him, brass-capped oil-canisters line a wall of pigeonholes, each tagged with a household name in a fine spidering hand. A wide staircase rises to the upper room where the senior council meets; the lower stairs go down to the rendering cellars, and the smell from below is sharper, animal, when the door is left open. Visitors are offered tea in pewter cups and asked to wait.

At the foot of Pier Three squats a building of grey granite with a brass weathervane shaped like a gull holding a key. The double doors are heavy oak banded in iron, propped open in fair weather; inside, a flagged entry hall opens onto a circular council room where five high-backed chairs face a low table strewn with permits, ledgers, and a brass bell. The walls carry framed harbor charts going back nine generations, and a long window looks out over the wharves and the Reach beyond. The clerk's desk is to the left of the door, the petitioner's bench to the right. The light here is honest daylight by day and Guild-tallow by night; the air smells of beeswax polish, ink, and the cold draught off the water.

A four-storey building of soot-darkened brick stands at the landward end of Pier Two, its ground floor given over to the public counter where cargo manifests are stamped and harbor dues recorded. Wooden benches line the walls; clerks in dark sleeve-protectors work behind a brass grille. A back staircase climbs past the second floor — storage for confiscated goods — to the third and fourth, where the crown auditor and her clerks have taken rooms. The upper windows look down on the wharves; a thin smoke rises from a chimney that serves both the clerks' stove and the auditor's modest hearth. The smell is of ink, damp wool, sealing wax, and the faint vinegar tang of the preservative used on the older ledgers.

Set into the lane behind the rope-walks, the Saltgull is a low-beamed public house with a black-painted door and a swinging sign carved with a gull breaking a chain. Inside, a long bar of scarred elm runs the length of one wall; the other holds a fireplace that burns peat brought down from the moors. Tables are mismatched, the floor is sanded fresh each morning, and the rafters hang with old fishing floats, dried herbs, and one preserved gull's wing that no one will explain. Patrons keep their voices low. The light is rendered tallow in the wall-sconces and a single fish-oil lamp behind the bar — a deliberate distinction the regulars notice. Smells of peat smoke, fish stew, dark beer, and wet wool.

A woman in her early thirties, slight and quick-moving, dressed in the practical leathers of a working fisher with an oilskin hat pushed back on her head. Her hair is the dark red of wet kelp; freckles cross the bridge of her nose. Her hands are calloused and stained with tar at the knuckles. She speaks fast, in the Underpiers cadence, with sentences that tail off into laughs when she's pleased and into silences when she's not. She carries a short gutting knife in a sheath at the small of her back and a small oilskin packet — her personal salt-ledger — inside her shirt against her ribs.

At the seaward end of the Underpiers, where the boardwalks give out into open mudflat at low tide, the burned stump of Pier Four leans drunkenly into the channel. Three blackened pilings still stand above the waterline; the rest are stubs that show only at the lowest tides. A small shrine of weathered planks has been built on the surviving boards at the landward end — bundles of dried fish, coils of rope, and chalked names cover the inner walls. Crabs work the mudflat below. The air here smells of deep brine, charred wood, and the bog-grass burned in the shrine's brazier. When the tide comes in, the water rises fast and quiet, and the shrine becomes an island.

A raised wooden platform under the second tier of the Underpiers' main boardwalk, reached by a short ramp that floods first when the tide comes in. The stall is roofed in tarred canvas and walled on three sides with slat-board; the front opens onto the walkway, where a long table displays the day's catch on beds of damp seaweed. Mer Tallow works behind the table on a stool worn smooth by decades. Knives hang on a leather strip above her head; a brass scale swings from a beam. A waterproof chest sits bolted to the platform behind her, padlocked, its lid scarred with old salt-rings. The smell is gut, brine, and the green note of fresh-cut seaweed.

Three flights up a leaning tenement stair on the eastern edge of the Underpiers, behind a door painted the dull green of old copper, is a single room with a sleeping platform slung from the ceiling and a stove vented through a tin pipe. A window the size of a hand opens on the channel; a desk made from a salvaged ship's locker holds a stack of oilskin-wrapped notebooks, a pencil-stub, a tallow lamp that has not been lit in fifteen years, and a fish-oil one that has. The walls are bare except for a single nail from which hangs a brass-capped oil-canister, empty, its strap cut clean through.

On the bluff's seaward edge stands a white tower banded in three rings of black, ninety feet from base to gallery. The lower door is iron-bound oak, set into a stone keeper's cottage that hunches against the tower's landward side. The cottage has a slate roof, two windows of thick green glass, and a chimney that smokes thinly in all weathers. Inside, a spiral stair of cast iron climbs the tower past the oil store, the keeper's workshop, and the lower gallery to the lamp-rooms at the top. The inner lamp still turns in its housing, its rendered tallow burning the familiar blue-amber, sweeping the estuary mouth. Above it, in a separate housing on the seaward face, the outer lamp's reflector sits dark and cold. The whole tower smells of polished brass, lamp-oil, and the chalk dust the wind scours off the bluff.

Set back from the high street behind a wall of grey stone topped with iron spikes, the residence is a two-storey house of dressed granite with a slate roof and tall sash windows that look down over the Pier District to the harbor. A walled garden wraps the seaward side, planted in salt-tolerant herbs and a single old apple tree leaning toward the cliff. The front door is painted a faded crown-blue. A brass plate beside the bell reads MORROW in letters worn nearly smooth. Inside, the front parlour is plain — dark wood, a peat fire, a long table where the Harbormaster takes private meetings — and the upstairs is private to the family. The garden gate opens onto a path that runs along the bluff to the lighthouse.

At the inland end of the Upper Town's high street stands a low chapel of pale stone, its roof a single sweep of slate, its door always unlocked. Inside, twenty-three small carved figures — half-scale replicas of the Saints on the breakwater — stand in niches along both walls. Each niche holds a brass lamp that burns rendered tallow from dusk to dawn. The floor is flagged in worn slate; the air carries beeswax, tallow smoke, and the dry-grass smell of the woven mats the moor-folk leave as offerings. A single bench faces the altar, which holds nothing but a length of tarred rope coiled in a clay dish. The wind here is constant and audible — it moves through the bell-cote above as a low continuous hum.

A shallow bowl in the moor's high heath holds seventeen monoliths leaning in a rough oval against the wind. The stones are dark, lichen-mottled, and head-and-a-half taller than a tall man at their fullest. Heather grows thick around their bases; sheep paths thread between them. At the eastern edge of the oval, a single low cottage of moor-stone and turf squats against the wind, its chimney smoking thinly. From the centre of the oval, on a clear day, one can see the lighthouse on its bluff to the west and the dark line of the Drowning Reach beyond. The wind here has a particular note — a low whistle through the pine-stands below — that gives the moors their name.

Where the old drove road from the inland farms crosses the cart-track down to Coldhaven, a low stone marker leans at the verge, its face carved with a worn symbol — a knot inside a circle. Beside it stands a small open-sided shelter of pine planks, roofed in turf, with a stone bench inside. A water trough is cut into the rock beside the shelter, fed by a thin spring that runs clear in all weathers. Three black pines stand close enough to whistle in the wind. From here the moors fall away westward toward the harbor, the lighthouse just visible on its bluff; eastward the road climbs into the heath. Moor-folk pause here on market days to rest the donkeys and eat bread.

A long shallow bank in the Drowning Reach, roughly two miles seaward of the breakwater, where the bottom rises within a fathom of the surface at low water. The bank is unmarked by buoy but well known by feel — the swell shortens, the colour of the water lightens to a sour green, and gulls work the surface for the small fish driven up from the deeper channel either side. In fog the Tallowback is invisible until a hull grinds on it. Boats avoid it by tradition, taking the channel north or south. With the outer lamp dark, captains crossing the Reach have begun to find the bank in ways they had not previously.

At roughly the midpoint of the Saints' Walk, one of the carved figures stands taller than the others — a robed shape with deep-set eye sockets carved as empty hollows, its mouth a thin straight line. The stone is darker here than the surrounding granite, weathered into a different texture, as though it was set into the breakwater later than its neighbours. A small brass lamp burns at its base from dusk to soft hour. The flagstones in front of the niche are worn smooth by foot traffic; children dare each other to reach up and touch the figure's face, and many have. Offerings accumulate at its feet — coils of rope, dried fish, occasionally a folded paper with a name written on it.

Halfway along the Saints' Walk, set into a granite recess on the harbor-facing side of the breakwater, a small wooden hut shelters a stack of brass oil-canisters, a lantern-pole, a coil of waxed rope, and a bench wide enough for two. The door is unlocked and bears a single chalk mark — a tally renewed each evening. From the bench one can see the entire arc of the breakwater, the Pier District lights, and on clear nights the lighthouse's inner beam sweeping the estuary. The hut smells of tallow, brass polish, and the salt that gets into everything. A small slate hangs from a nail inside, where the wicktender on duty notes the time each Saint's lamp was lit.

A thin courteous man in his sixties, narrow-shouldered in unmarked grey wool, his hair gone iron-grey and combed back from a high forehead. He moves slowly through the Guildhall's lower rooms with the small steady tread of someone who has measured these floorboards for forty years. His voice is soft and even; he never raises it and rarely needs to. He carries his brass-capped oil-canister at his hip like an old habit even when there is no reason. When he listens he tilts his head a fraction to the left and does not interrupt; when he speaks, he chooses words as though each costs him a coin. The faint smell of rendered tallow follows him everywhere.

A competent tired woman in her fifties, broad-shouldered under a dark wool coat cut crown-formal but mended at the cuffs. Her hair is the colour of wet sand, pulled back into a knot that loosens by the end of each council day. She walks with a slight favour of the right knee — an old dock injury — and carries her brass keys on a chain at her belt. Her voice is low and carries; she has the habit of pausing a full beat before answering a question, watching the petitioner's face. When she is tired her vowels flatten toward the moor-side accent of her mother's family. She drinks tea constantly and eats very little in public.

A small precise woman in her early forties, dressed in the dark crown-cloth of her office — high-collared coat, narrow skirt, polished boots that show every speck of mud the Pier District puts on them. Her hair is black, cut short under a flat crown-cap. She wears wire-framed spectacles she removes when she wants to make a point. Her voice is clipped, her accent inland-northern, her manner unfailingly polite and entirely unbending. She carries a leather satchel of writs at all times, even to dinner. When she examines a ledger she does so with a brass straight-edge, and she takes notes in a cipher of her own devising.

A heavyset woman in her late sixties, broad in the shoulder from a lifetime of gutting fish, her grey hair cropped short under a tarred canvas cap. Her hands are scarred white from knife-work and old burns; her arms are bare to the elbow in all weathers. She works behind her stall on a stool worn smooth by decades, knife moving in a steady rhythm that does not pause when she speaks. Her voice is rough and carrying. She makes eye contact directly and at length, and her laugh — when it comes, which is not often — is sudden and loud. She wears a small iron knot on a leather cord at her throat.

A wiry man in his late fifties, weathered to the colour of tea-stained paper, with deep-set eyes and a habit of looking past the person he's speaking to. He dresses in patched dark wool and goes bareheaded. His left hand is missing the last two fingers — an old wicktender's accident, he says, when asked, which is rarely. He moves quietly even on the Underpiers' loud boardwalks. His voice when he uses it is dry and unhurried, with the particular cadence of someone who once recited the same route every dusk for thirty years. He does not drink in public houses, but he will accept tea standing at a doorway.

A tall woman in her late thirties, lean and wind-burned, her dark hair cut at jaw-length and bleached at the tips by salt. She wears the keeper's heavy oilskin coat and tarred canvas trousers tucked into sea-boots, even indoors. Her eyes are pale grey and slow to settle on anything; she has the long-distance focus of someone who has spent years looking at horizons. She speaks little, in a quiet voice with the Upper Town's clipped vowels. When she descends to the Pier District for supplies she does so at dawn and leaves before the wicktenders' morning round. She is rarely seen smiling and is not known to drink in company.

A small straight-backed woman in her sixties, robed in the undyed wool of the Breakwater Saints' clergy, a length of tarred rope worn as a belt. Her face is weathered fine, her hair white and braided close to the skull. She moves between the figures of the inland shrine with a practiced economy, trimming each lamp's wick without looking, refilling each reservoir in turn. Her voice when she leads a service is low and clear; when she speaks privately it is hardly more than a whisper. She wears no rings. She has the moor-folk's flatter vowel beneath her crown-trained pronunciation, surfacing when she is tired.

A small grey woman of indeterminate age, somewhere between sixty and ninety, wrapped in undyed wool and a moor-cloak pinned at the throat with a knot of iron. Her hair is the colour of weathered bone; her eyes are pale and direct. She walks the Standing Field with a hazel staff that she also uses to measure the lean of each stone. Her voice is quiet and carries the moor's flat vowel without the polishing of crown-schooling. She does not come down to Coldhaven herself — she sends younger moor-folk on market days — but she will receive visitors at her cottage if they have walked up under their own power and brought no Guild oil with them.

A young man of perhaps nineteen, sandy-haired and sharp-featured, in the unmarked grey wool of a wicktender with the leather strap of his brass canister fresh and stiff across his chest. He walks his route at a steady pace, head turning constantly — taking in lit windows, unlit ones, the chalk-marks on doorframes. He greets householders by name and asks after their elders. His laugh comes easily, his eyes do not. He carries a small notebook in his coat pocket and writes in it after each house. He stops at the Saltgull for half a pint at the end of his evening round and exchanges words with the keeper that no one else can hear.

A heavyset man in his late forties, ruddy-faced, dressed in the leather apron of the Saltgull's keeper over a clean linen shirt. His hands are huge and surprisingly gentle on the pewter mugs. He moves behind his bar with the economy of someone who has stood there for twenty-five years and knows every plank's give. His voice is a low rumble; he laughs at customers' jokes without seeming to find them funny. He keeps his eyes on the door and on the fish-oil lamp behind the bar in roughly equal measure. He does not drink with patrons but pours himself a small dark beer at the end of each night, alone, after the last regular leaves.

A child of perhaps eight years, slight, pale-haired, dressed now in the patched wool the Underpiers women have made for her — but standing as though she still expects different clothes. She does not blink as often as a child should. Her skin has the faint blue-grey undertone of someone who has been cold for a very long time. Her hair is dry and lies flat to her skull. She watches adults' faces with a steady attention that does not look like a child's curiosity. When she speaks — which is rarely, and only to those who have earned it by sitting with her in silence first — her vowels are wrong, the consonants softer, the grammar arranged around what scholars would recognise as dead dialect. She smells faintly of cold deep brine.

A stooped man in his eighties, all knuckles and elbows under a moth-eaten scholar's gown, peering through thick spectacles that he wipes constantly on a square of grey linen. His hair is a thin white fringe; his teeth are mostly his own. He moves between the shelves of the Council's archive with a candle-stub in a small tin shield, having refused on principle to allow the room to be fitted with Guild tallow-lamps. His voice is high and dry. He laughs often, at his own observations, in a sound like a sheet of paper tearing. He smells of old vellum, candle-wax, and the violet-pastilles he sucks against a chronic cough.

A neat compact woman in her thirties, in the dark crown-cloth of an auditor's clerk, hair pinned tight under a small cap. She wears ink-guards on both sleeves and a steel-nibbed pen behind her ear at all times. Her movements are precise and rapid; she eats standing up at the customs house window when she eats at all. Her voice is quiet and accentless in the crown-trained way. She takes the Saltgull's evening meal with her colleagues but does not drink with them, and she has been observed several times watching the back room's door for longer than politeness requires.

Solen Vare is a road-weary cartographer in his middle years, a former ship's surveyor who lost the Crestline Maren on the estuary rocks one fog-blind autumn night when the outer lamp was already dark. He came ashore the only one of his crew to make it unassisted, took cheap lodgings in the Underpiers because its residents asked the fewest questions, and has been mapping the harbor district for coin ever since — for a merchant's insurance dispute first, then quietly for the Harbormaster's Council itself.

He does not consider himself an investigator. He is a man who cannot leave a chart unfinished, and the margins of his working maps have begun accumulating notes that have nothing to do with distances: which households burn rendered tallow and which burn something cheaper, which doors go unanswered during the Estuary Hours, where brine-sealed chests have surfaced. Somewhere in his grid of pier measurements and lantern-counts is a pattern he has not yet named, and in Coldhaven that may be the most dangerous kind of map to be drawing.

Every street in the Pier District is lit by Guild lanterns burning rendered tallow. A household whose lantern is dim or unlit is publicly marked as out of standing — neighbors will cross the street rather than walk past it, and creditors will call the following morning.

Beneath the customs house at Pier Three are vaulted brick cellars used for bonded goods awaiting tithe assessment. The crown auditor has taken rooms above them and ordered three cellar doors sealed pending inspection — doors the Guild would prefer she not open.

A short tunnel runs from a disused coal-chute in the Council chambers directly into the Guildhall's lower archive. It is not on any plan and exists so that quiet conversations between Harbormaster and Guild Master never need to cross a public street.

The Pier District is laid out along three working piers numbered seaward — Pier One handles passenger traffic and the small ferry, Pier Two the fishing fleet, Pier Three customs and bonded warehousing. The Guildhall stands at the inland end of Pier Two, deliberately equidistant from the Council chambers and the customs house.

Twice daily the Underpiers floods to roughly four feet. During the Hours, no formal name-transfer may be conducted by Guild convention, no Council writ may be served, and most business pauses. Residents call the slack period between floods 'the dry watch.'
The collapsed fourth pier, abandoned a generation ago after a storm, juts seaward as a ruin of black pilings. Most Returnings in recent years have happened on its mudflats at the turn of the tide.

The child who walked out of the surf is sheltered in a raised room above a net-mender's shop in the deep Unders. She has not aged in the eleven months she has been there and speaks only dead dialect. The household has not reported her to the Guild.

Several Underpiers households maintain interlinked salt-ledgers, copying entries between them so that no single fire or Guild seizure can erase the record. The oldest ledger is kept by a fishmonger called Mer Tallow and goes back three generations.

Lodges in a rented room in the Underpiers because it was the cheapest district and because its residents, accustomed to things that Return from the water, ask fewer questions than anyone else in Coldhaven.

The current keeper is a woman called Adwen Roak, third of her line in the post. She has offered no public explanation for the outer lamp's extinction and has stopped attending Council meetings, though she still admits the wicktender who fills the inner lamp's reservoir.

A small stone chapel above the bluff holds the indoor companions to the breakwater figures — older carvings, said to be the originals from which the breakwater Saints were copied. Offerings of rope and salt are still left at the door.

Adwen Roak knows precisely why the outer lamp went out. She extinguished it herself, after reading the sealed letter she opened on her elevation to keeper six years ago. She has offered no public explanation and has stopped attending Council meetings.

Seventeen stones in a rough oval on the high heath, maintained by a hereditary line of stone-tenders. The Moors Compact obliges them to keep the stones upright, mossed in particular patterns, and circled by a cut firebreak each spring.
The Moors supply timber for pier repair, peat for cooking fires, and a particular bog-herb called fennow that is rendered into Guild lamp-oil. The fennow trade is the Compact's economic spine.

During spring tides and the new moon, certain of the standing stones produce a low audible hum that the stone-tenders treat as a working condition, not an omen. They adjust the moss patterns in response.

The stones do not 'hold the fog from the high ground' metaphorically; they hold something specific. The eldest stone-tender, Ifor Penny, can name what — a thing the Compact's original language called a 'far-listener' — and knows that two stones have shifted out of alignment this year.

In the past year, at least nine corpses, four sealed chests, a wooden saint's-figure missing from the breakwater two centuries ago, and one living child have come ashore from the Reach. The Guild has acquired most of them under salvage convention.

A merchant brig called the Antrine sank on the Tallowback eighty years ago carrying, among other cargo, the Guild's previous Ledger of Absences. The current Ledger is its replacement — and the older one may now be returning, page by page, in the sealed chests.

A long shallow bank two miles offshore where the water turns oddly still even in heavy weather. Fishers do not cast nets over it; the reason given is that the catch comes up wrong — too perfect, too cold. The bank is a mile offshore at its nearest point.

The Crestline Maren, a coastal survey brig, broke up on the estuary rocks just inside the breakwater roughly a year ago on a moonless autumn night. The outer lamp was dark that night — months before the town acknowledged its extinction. Only the ship's cartographer Solen Vare reached shore unassisted.

Twenty-three carved figures, each with a local name — the Knot-Keeper, the Hollow-Eyed, the One Who Counts, the Salt-Mouth, and so on. Their crown-canonical identities, if any, have been forgotten; the local names are the only ones in use.

The Guild lights a small lamp at the base of each Saint every dusk. This is not Council-mandated; it is a Guild practice that has acquired the force of ritual. A Saint left unlit is considered a very bad sign.

At the far end of the Walk is a weathered stone socket where a twenty-fourth Saint once stood. No one currently living remembers what figure occupied it, and the Ledger of Absences has a page corresponding to it that is, on inspection, blank but warm to the touch.

Maintains the town's lantern network, sells rendered tallow, collects oil-tithes monthly through wicktenders, and adjudicates disputes between members. Officially a chartered trade guild under a forty-year-old Council license.

Guild Master Ovin Cawl has led the Guild for nineteen years. His deputy and likely successor is Mistress Brenna Voss, who oversees the Ledger of Absences and is widely considered the actual operational head.

The Guild's most lucrative business is brokering half-remembered names — collecting them from the dying and the grieving, recording them in the Ledger, and selling them as sealed names to clients in Coldhaven and certain inland buyers. The trade is an open secret locally and entirely unknown to the crown.

The Guild's master record sits in the inner sanctum of the Guildhall, in a locked room only the Master, the Deputy, and the senior archivist may enter. Pages have begun adding themselves overnight in the past year — entries in hands no current Guild member recognizes.

The Guild's official position is that name-hunger does not exist and is a folk superstition of the Underpiers. Senior lamplighters know better; they keep a private list of fully-sold clients and quietly buy back fragments of those names when name-hunger becomes incapacitating.

The Guild has known for at least three generations that the outer lamp's continuous burning was part of an arrangement with the keepers' line — not a navigational duty but a containment. Master Cawl received the briefing on his elevation and has been in panicked private correspondence with Adwen Roak since the lamp went out.

Five seats: Harbormaster, two senior guild merchants (currently chandler Ren Halbrook and rope-maker Tomas Veere), one clergy representative (Sister Onella Drake of the Saints' shrine), and one rotating fishing-cooperative seat (currently held by the Tallowback Cooperative).

Civil and criminal authority over commerce, the harbor, and public order. May issue writs, hang for capital crimes, and license trades. Has no formal authority over the Naming Trade — the Council's charter does not mention names at all.

The Harbormaster's own family carries a notorious Tide Debt — a great-uncle and a brother both lost to the water decades apart. Iselt Morrow has begun, quietly, to fear that one or both will Return on her watch, and her judgments have been subtly shaped by that anticipation.

Harbormaster Morrow uses the unmarked passage between the Council chambers and the Guildhall archive approximately twice a month. She believes she controls the relationship; the Guild's records of those meetings suggest otherwise.

Was hired first by a merchant for pier measurements in an insurance dispute, then quietly retained by the Harbormaster's Council for a supplementary harbor survey after the Council discovered their own charts predated the last major pier collapse by two decades.

Quietly commissioned a supplementary harbor survey from the shipwrecked cartographer Solen Vare after discovering the Council's working charts predated the last major pier collapse by two decades. The commission is paid from the Harbormaster's discretionary purse rather than from minuted Council funds.

To assess three generations of unpaid harbor levies, audit the town's commercial books, and produce a report to the crown treasury. Vane carries writs that could authorize military enforcement if she requests it, though she has not.

Coldhaven's books record debts owed to persons not in any crown registry, payments to unnamed accounts, and entries dated before the transactions they describe. Vane has filled two private notebooks with examples and has stopped sleeping well.

Auditor Vane has begun to suspect that the town's books and the Guild's Ledger of Absences are the same document kept in two registers, and that understanding one requires reading the other. She has not requested access yet because she is not certain what she would do with permission.

Each salt-ledger is kept in oilskin, written in pencil, and copied at irregular intervals to two or three other ledgers. No central index exists. To know who keeps which ledger, you must already be trusted by someone who does.

The Circle has developed a procedure for things that Return at Pier Four: identification by salt-ledger first, Guild notification second (or never), and a quiet network of safe rooms for Returnings that should not be handed over.

The Circle is sheltering the child who walked out of the surf. Mer Tallow has been slowly recording, in dead dialect transliteration, the things the child says — and has realized in the past month that the child is naming people who have been sold through the Naming Trade.

Guarantees moor-folk free access to Coldhaven's market and exempts them from oil-tithe. In exchange, the stone-tenders maintain certain stones on the moor. The original document is lost; the Guild claims it is in the Ledger of Absences.
Timber, peat, mutton, undyed wool, and the bog-herb fennow that goes into Guild lamp-oil. Without fennow, rendered tallow burns yellow instead of Guild-light blue-amber.

Ifor Penny can read enough dead dialect to parse the Compact's original language. She has never told the Guild that she can, and she has known for some years that the Compact's obligations run in both directions — the Guild owes the stones something it has stopped delivering.

The seventeen stones contain — or contain the attention of — what the old language calls a far-listener, a presence in the deep water that hears names spoken on land. Two stones have shifted this year. Ifor Penny believes the outer lamp's extinction is connected and is preparing to walk down to Coldhaven for the first time in eleven years.

Three centuries ago, the founding Keepers bargained with a presence in the deep water — the far-listener — to take the town's forgotten names in exchange for not taking its remembered ones. The outer lamp, the Ledger, and the stones are the three instruments of that bargain.
Adwen Roak (lighthouse), Ovin Cawl (Guild), Onella Drake (shrine). None of the three trusts the other two completely; all three know the arrangement is failing.

Adwen Roak extinguished the outer lamp on instructions from her grandmother, who came to believe the bargain had become parasitic — that the far-listener was no longer accepting forgotten names as payment but was using the Ledger to identify and call back remembered ones. The Returnings are the call being answered. Roak believes ending the bargain is worth whatever comes next.
Houses the Lamplighters' Guild's administrative offices, oil-tithe collection desks, and rendering cellars where the proprietary tallow is processed.
The senior council of seven meets in the upper room every fourth night. The stairs to it are guarded by a wicktender who knows every full member by sight.
The Ledger of Absences is kept in an iron-bound cabinet in a windowless room behind the upper council chamber. Only the Guild Master and two named lamplighters hold keys.
Junior clerks have been quietly told to report any morning when the Ledger appears thicker than it was the previous night. Three such reports have come in since midsummer.
The Council sits in open session every Tideday morning and in closed session whenever the Harbormaster calls it. Petitioners may speak in open session if their name is on the day's list.

The brass bell on the council table is rung once to open session, twice to silence the room, and three times to suspend a session on grounds of Estuary Hours — no formal business may be conducted during the Hours.

Harbormaster Morrow's private office holds a locked drawer containing letters from her predecessor warning her not to inquire into the outer lamp's keepers. She has read them twice and replaced them carefully.
Records all cargo entering and leaving Coldhaven harbor and collects crown harbor dues — three generations of which are currently in arrears.
Auditor Sera Vane and three crown clerks occupy the upper two floors. They take meals sent up from the Saltgull and rarely descend to the public counter.

The third-floor archive holds harbor ledgers going back over two centuries. Entries before the Guild's founding use a different hand and reference accounts that have no names attached — only sealed marks.
Frequented by pier-workers, off-duty wicktenders, occasional moor-folk on market days, and — recently — clerks of the crown auditor's office who take their meals here.
The single fish-oil lamp behind the bar is lit every evening before the tallow sconces are touched. Asking why earns a shrug from the keeper and silence from the regulars.
The Salt-Ledger Circle uses the back room on certain evenings, signalled by the fish-oil lamp being moved to the bar's far end. The keeper takes no part but charges nothing for the room.
Most things that Return — corpses, sealed chests, and once a child — first appear here, washed up against the burned pilings on the rising tide.

The shrine is tended by no one in particular and everyone in general. Underpiers residents add names to its walls when someone is lost to the water. Names sometimes appear that no one remembers chalking.

Pier Four burned in a fire forty years ago that the Guild's records describe as accidental. The salt-ledgers describe it differently — as the night a lamplighter walked the pier with a torch and a list.
Sells the day's catch — mostly cod, mackerel, and the small grey crabs the Underpiers calls 'tithe-pinchers' — at prices set in conference with the other Unders fishmongers each dawn.
Underpiers residents pass news through Tallow's stall by long habit. To 'leave word at Mer's' is to put it into the Unders' communal memory.
The padlocked chest behind the stall holds Mer Tallow's salt-ledger — the oldest continuous one in the Underpiers, with entries going back to her grandmother's hand.

Arrived at Mer Tallow's stall at the mouth of the Underpiers ostensibly to price passage out and settle some small debts, but the tide is wrong and the Tallowback has been grounding boats that should know better.
Joss Pell, retired wicktender, has lived here since he left the Guild fifteen years ago.
The oilskin-wrapped notebooks on the desk contain Pell's reconstruction of his old wicktender route — every household, every oil-tithe, every lantern-debt he can remember from his Guild years.
The brass-capped canister on the wall is the one Pell carried as a wicktender. He cut the strap with his own knife the night he walked away. He has not said why to anyone, including Mer Tallow.
The inner lamp guides ships through the estuary mouth and continues to burn. It is fuelled with standard Guild-rendered tallow delivered weekly.
The outer lamp has been dark since midsummer. Keeper Adwen Roak has offered no public explanation. The Guild has not been permitted to inspect the housing.
The outer lamp was never fuelled by rendered tallow. Its housing holds a different reservoir whose contents the lighthouse line has kept private for three centuries.
Adwen Roak extinguished the outer lamp deliberately after reading the sealed letter she opened on her elevation. She has told no one in Coldhaven what the letter said.

Came ashore alive the night the Crestline Maren broke up on the estuary rocks — the only crew member to reach land without help. The outer lamp was dark that night, months before the town officially noticed its extinction, and Vare has replayed the geometry of the wreck so often it has become a navigational problem rather than a memory.
Harbormaster Iselt Morrow lives here with her aging mother and a single housekeeper. Her two grown children have moved inland.
The garden gate connects to a cliff path that leads directly to the lighthouse cottage. Morrow's predecessors used it; she has walked it twice in eleven years.

The salt-ledgers note that the Morrow family carries an old Tide Debt — something went into the water in her great-grandfather's time and has not yet come back. The current recent Returnings have her watching the surf with quiet care.
Tended by Sister Onella Drake and two lay assistants. Open at all hours; services are held at dawn and dusk.
The twenty-three figures inside mirror the twenty-three Saints on the breakwater. Their carvings are older than the chapel and were moved here from somewhere else within living memory.
The rope coiled on the altar is replaced every spring by Sister Drake personally. The old rope is burned, not buried — a detail Drake will not explain.
Drake keeps her Keeper's sealed letter behind a loose flagstone beneath the altar's clay dish. She has opened it; she has told no one, including the other Keepers, what it said.
Seventeen monoliths, leaning in an oval. Local tradition holds that the original arrangement was nineteen; two have fallen and not been replaced within living memory.
The stone-tender's cottage at the field's edge is occupied by Ifor Penny. She has lived there for as long as anyone in Coldhaven can remember.
The oval's long axis is oriented precisely toward where the outer lamp burns from the lighthouse — or did, until midsummer. The stones' lean tracks this alignment within a few degrees.

The two missing monoliths fell sixty and ninety years ago respectively. Their stumps are visible in the heather. Ifor Penny has tried twice in her tenure to raise replacements and been prevented — once by storm, once by the moor-folk themselves.
A traditional resting point on the moor-folk's fortnightly journey down to Coldhaven market. The shelter is maintained communally by the farmstead families.
The carved stone bears the symbol of the Moors Compact — a knot inside a circle. Moor-folk touch it on passing; harbor-folk who use the road generally do not.
The spring beneath the trough has never failed in living memory. Ifor Penny has been seen leaving small offerings — a coin, a pinch of salt — at its source on certain nights of the year.
The Tallowback rises to within a fathom of the surface at lowest water. A draught of more than four feet will ground on it.
Captains have traditionally fixed their position relative to the Tallowback by the bearing of the outer lamp from the lighthouse. With the lamp dark, three boats have grounded on it since midsummer.

On the bank's seaward edge lies the keel of an old vessel, deep enough to be invisible at all tides but shallow enough to foul a dragged net. The salt-ledgers name it the Onella, which is not a name in any harbor register.
Called the Hollow-Eyed in local tradition. One of twenty-three Breakwater Saints. Its empty eye-sockets are the deepest of any figure on the Walk.

Folded papers left at its feet typically bear the name of someone the leaver wishes to remember — or, less often, someone they wish to forget. The papers are gathered each dawn by a wicktender and burned at the lighthouse.

The Hollow-Eyed's stone is not granite. It does not match any quarry in the region. The figure was set into the breakwater at the breakwater's original construction and predates the other Saints by an unknown interval.
Used by the wicktender on Saints' Walk duty as a shelter and re-supply point during the nightly lamp-lighting round.
The slate inside records the time each of the twenty-three Saints' lamps was lit. The wicktender on duty signs it with their initials.

For the last three months, the lamp at the Hollow-Eyed's niche has been recorded as lit on the slate but has been found dark by dawn more nights than not. No wicktender has reported this to senior Guild members.
Guild Master of the Lamplighters' Guild. Has held the post for nineteen years.
Famously soft-spoken. Conducts even adversarial negotiations over tea, in the upper room, with the door closed.
Last of the Cawl line in Coldhaven. Unmarried, no acknowledged children. Lives alone in apartments above the Guildhall's east wing.
Cawl is one of the three hereditary Keepers of the Outer Lamp. He inherited the role on his father's death and opened the sealed letter that night.

Cawl is aware that pages have been adding themselves to the Ledger of Absences and has not reported this to the senior council. He has begun reading the new pages alone, by tallow-light, after midnight.
Harbormaster of Coldhaven and chair of the Harbormaster's Council. Eleven years in the seat.
Of the old Morrow line, which has held harbor offices in three of the last six generations. Widowed; two grown children living inland.
Has met privately with Auditor Vane four times since the auditor's arrival. The meetings are not minuted. Both women drink the same tea.
Knows her family carries an old Tide Debt — her great-grandfather drowned with something the salt-ledgers will not name. She watches the Pier Four returns more closely than her position requires.

Personally commissioned the shipwrecked cartographer Solen Vare to re-chart the harbor district, with particular interest in the Pier Four mudflats. She has reviewed his drafts in her private office and paid him in coin from her own purse on at least one occasion.
Crown auditor dispatched to assess and collect three generations of unpaid harbor levies. Lodged in the upper rooms of the customs house with three clerks.
Treated with elaborate civility and complete obstruction by every Coldhaven institution. She has noted this in her private correspondence with the crown.

Has identified consistent patterns in the harbor books that should not be possible — payments to unnamed accounts, debts predicting events. She has not yet written this up formally because she does not believe her own conclusions.

Vane's elder sister disappeared from a different coastal town twelve years ago. She has never spoken of it professionally. She accepted this assignment because the patterns in Coldhaven's books match patterns in her sister's last letter.
Senior fishmonger of the Underpiers. Has worked the same stall since she was sixteen; took it over from her mother.
Treated by Underpiers residents as a community elder. News passes through her stall; disputes are settled in her hearing.
Keeps the oldest continuous salt-ledger in the Underpiers, started by her grandmother. The chest behind her stall holds three generations of entries.
The knot at her throat is a Moors Compact token, given to her by Ifor Penny twenty years ago. Mer Tallow is the only harbor-side person to wear one openly.
Retired wicktender. Walked the eastern Pier District route for thirty-one years before leaving the Guild fifteen years ago.
Quietly reconstructs his old route's lantern-debts and oil-tithes in private notebooks. Trusted by the Salt-Ledger Circle as one of its closest things to an elder.

On a winter night fifteen years ago, Pell lit a lamp at a house whose oil-tithe had been formally suspended by the Guild. The next morning the household — a mother and two children — had been struck from the Ledger of Absences. He saw the empty pages himself before he walked out.
Has refused all Guild requests to inspect the outer lamp's housing since extinguishing it at midsummer. Will not discuss her reasons in public.

One of the three hereditary Keepers. The lighthouse line holds the operative seal — extinguishing the lamp was her unilateral act, made after reading the letter she opened on her elevation six years ago.

The sealed letter told Roak that the outer lamp's purpose is the inverse of what the Guild believes — that for three centuries it has been calling, not warding. She has waited six years for evidence before acting on it. The recent Returnings provided the evidence.
Lighthouse keeper of Coldhaven. Inherited the post from her father, who inherited it from his mother. The Roak line has held the lighthouse for at least four generations.
Senior clergy of the inland shrine of the Breakwater Saints. Sits on the Harbormaster's Council as the clergy representative.
Born to a moor farmstead family; trained at the crown seminary inland; returned to Coldhaven at her elder's request thirty years ago.
Burns the previous year's altar rope each spring at the lighthouse's base — not at the shrine. She walks up the bluff at dawn to do this, alone, and has done so for thirty springs.

The third hereditary Keeper. Opened her letter ten years ago and has waited since. She is the only Keeper to have read both the lighthouse line's letter and the Guild line's letter — she stole copies on her elevation and has told no one.
