Eldest stone-tender of the Standing Field. Effective authority among the moor-folk by their own quiet consent.
Holds the moor-folk's oral version of the Moors Compact in memory, passed from her predecessor in a ritual the moor-folk do not discuss with outsiders.
Has lived in the tender's cottage for as long as anyone in Coldhaven can remember. Pier District residents who saw her as children describe her looking exactly as she looks now.

Knows the name the moor-folk give to what the lighthouse line called 'the far-listener,' and knows that the outer lamp's three-century arrangement was a containment, not a courtesy. She has been waiting for a Keeper to grasp this. Adwen Roak's extinguishing of the lamp surprised and grieved her.
Wicktender on the western Pier District route. Apprenticed to the Guild at twelve, full wicktender at seventeen.
Considered diligent and ambitious. Senior lamplighters have begun mentioning his name for advancement.

His notebook contains his official Guild observations. He keeps a second notebook, identical in appearance, hidden in a floorboard under his bed. The second one contains observations he passes verbally to Joss Pell once a fortnight.

Brann is the wicktender on Saints' Walk duty three nights in seven. He is the one signing the slate at the Hollow-Eyed's niche when the lamp does not stay lit. He has not reported the failures because he does not yet understand them.
Keeper of the Saltgull Tavern. Inherited the house from his uncle; has run it for twenty-five years.
Famously discreet. Does not repeat what he overhears, does not ask follow-up questions, does not look at the back-room door when it closes.
Allows the Salt-Ledger Circle to use his back room and signals their meetings by moving the fish-oil lamp. Takes no part in their work and asks for nothing in return.

Coel's wife's name was sold through the Naming Trade four years ago to settle a lantern-debt he could not pay. She has been suffering name-hunger since. He has not forgiven the Guild, but he has also not done anything about it except move the lamp on the right nights.
Captain of the small fishing skiff Knot-Keeper, working out of the Underpiers' lower landing. Crew of two — her younger brother and a hired hand.

Has grounded twice on the Tallowback since midsummer. Did not lose the boat either time but lost the day's catch and a length of net. Speaks angrily about the dark outer lamp to anyone who will listen.

On the second grounding, in heavy fog, she saw something walking on the Tallowback's exposed crest — a figure in robes the colour of wet stone, head turned toward the lighthouse. She has told no one but Mer Tallow.
Has twice hired the Underpiers cartographer Solen Vare to take new soundings of the Tallowback since her groundings, wanting a working chart of how the bottom has shifted with the outer lamp dark.
Walked out of the surf at the Pier Four ruin one dawn in early spring. Was taken in by an Underpiers family who lost a child of similar age to the water two generations ago.

Speaks in dead dialect — the pre-Guild speech of the coast. The only person in Coldhaven who can partially parse her speech is the elderly scholar who keeps the Council's archive of pre-Guild marginalia.

The family who took her in did not give her a new name and did not ask for her old one. The salt-ledgers list her only as 'the child from Pier Four.' She has not offered a name, and she flinches visibly when asked.

She remembers the Coldhaven of three centuries ago — the original arrangement of nineteen standing stones, the breakwater before the Saints were set into it, and the name of the far-listener in its proper form. She has not yet decided whether to share any of this.
Archivist of the Harbormaster's Council. Maintains the pre-Guild ledgers and the marginalia collection in a back room of the Council Chambers.
The only living person in Coldhaven who can partially parse dead dialect, from forty years of work on pre-Guild marginalia. Has corresponded with two crown scholars on the topic, both now deceased.
Has been quietly visiting the Pier Four child once a fortnight since her arrival, taking down her speech in careful phonetic notation. Has not yet told Harbormaster Morrow what he has translated.
Senior clerk to Auditor Sera Vane. Has worked under Vane on three previous assignments.
Cracked the first layer of the pre-Guild harbor ledger's cipher within a fortnight of arrival. Vane has begun trusting her with confidential cross-references.

Has noted the Saltgull's fish-oil lamp moving on certain evenings and has correlated those evenings with gaps in the customs records. She has not yet reported this to Vane. She is waiting to see whether the Circle is an obstacle or an ally.
Human Ranger 1 (Sailor background). HP 12, AC 14. Spent seventeen years as a ship's cartographer on coastal survey contracts before the wreck of the Crestline Maren a year ago.

Narrates distances and bearings under his breath when anxious, notices when a lantern burns the wrong color before he notices almost anything else, and repays small kindnesses with precisely rendered sketches — doorways, rooflines, faces — as though accurate representation is the only currency he trusts.

Keeps his working charts in an oilskin roll and his marginal notes — lantern-colors, unanswered doors during Estuary Hours, sightings of brine-sealed chests — in a separate pocket notebook he has not shown to any client.

rows.description: The Guildhall serves as the Guild's seat of power, housing the inner sanctum where the Ledger of Absences is kept and where senior lamplighters conduct the most sensitive transactions of the Naming Trade.

The Guild's oil-tithe network and wicktender patrols give it effective surveillance and social authority over the Pier District's households and businesses, enforcing compliance through the threat of unlit lanterns.

The Guild maintains a precarious hold over the Underpiers through lantern-debt records and wicktender rounds, though the district's informal salt-ledger culture and proximity to Returning events make it the Guild's most resistant territory.

Though the Council nominally governs the town, it defers to the Guild on any matter touching names, debts, or the night. The Guild's leverage is informal but absolute — it holds lantern-debt records on most Councillors' families.

The Salt-Ledger Circle maintains a rival system of memory-keeping that tracks Tide Debts and Returning events outside Guild oversight. The Guild is deeply uncomfortable with this parallel accounting and watches the Circle's activities closely without yet moving openly against it.

The auditor's mandate to examine the town's books threatens to expose the Guild's practice of recording debts owed to persons who do not exist in any crown registry. The Guild is extremely sensitive about the distinction between oil-tithe and tax, and regards the audit as an existential threat.

Ovin Cawl is the Guild's senior master, responsible for the Ledger of Absences and the most sensitive transactions of the Naming Trade. He knows someone is selling true-names to outsiders and is conducting a quiet internal investigation he cannot afford to make public.

Iselt Morrow chairs the Council and is its most capable member, but her authority is bounded by the Guild's informal dominance. Her family carries a Tide Debt — something of the Morrows went into the water long ago — which makes her position doubly precarious as Returning events accelerate.

The Morrow family carries a Tide Debt — something of theirs went into the water long ago — and the Guild holds lantern-debt records on the family as well. Iselt's position as Harbormaster gives her nominal authority over the Guild, but her family's debts give the Guild leverage she cannot ignore.

Sera Vane is the crown's representative, holding writs that could theoretically authorize military force to collect three generations of unpaid harbor levies. She is not a military figure but is methodical and has begun to notice that the town's books record payments to accounts with no corresponding names.

Vane's audit of the harbor levies has led her into the Guild's financial records, where she finds entries made in anticipation of events that had not yet occurred and debts owed to persons who do not exist in any crown registry. She does not yet understand what the Naming Trade is, but she is beginning to suspect the books are not merely irregular.

Vane has requested meetings with Cawl as the Guild's senior master, and he has complied with surface courtesy while revealing nothing. Each meeting is a careful negotiation in which both parties pretend the other does not know what they know.

Mer is a trusted contributor to the Salt-Ledger Circle's communal record-keeping, passing information about Returning events and brine-sealed objects through the network of oilskin-wrapped ledgers that circulate among Underpiers residents.

Joss Pell's household carries lantern-debt across at least two generations, meaning the Guild holds his family's names as soft collateral. He is 'burning on credit' and knows it, which shapes every interaction he has with Guild members.

Sister Onella Drake holds the clergy seat on the Council, representing the old coastal religion whose saints line the breakwater. Her position gives her a formal voice in Council deliberations, though she is more interested in the theological implications of the Returning than in harbor levies.

Drake resents the Guild's ritual adoption of the Breakwater Saints, which she reads as appropriation of the old coastal religion for commercial and political purposes. The Guild, for its part, finds Drake's theological interest in the Returning inconvenient and potentially destabilizing.

Coel Marrin holds one of the senior guild merchant seats on the Council, representing commercial interests that are nominally independent of the Lamplighters' Guild but in practice deeply entangled with it through lantern-debt and the Naming Trade.

Penharrow visits the Inland Shrine to consult Drake's pre-crown texts, which contain the closest available translation of the Moors Compact's original language. The two have developed a cautious scholarly alliance around the question of what the Compact actually obligates each party to do.

The child emerged from the surf during the Estuary Hours in the Underpiers, speaking in dead dialect. They have not aged, carry no lantern-debt in the Guild's records, and appear in no salt-ledger prior to their return, which means they are either a true Returning or something the town has no category for.

Drake has spent more time with the surf-child than anyone else in town, attempting to parse the dead dialect through her pre-crown marginalia. The child's speech encodes assumptions about time and identity that Drake finds theologically destabilizing.

Hesker Caul is suspected within the Guild of being the one selling true-names to outsiders. The Guild knows but cannot prove it, and Caul's position within or adjacent to the Guild makes a direct accusation politically dangerous for Master Cawl.

Cawl's quiet internal investigation has focused on Caul as the most likely source of the true-name leaks, but the evidence is circumstantial and Caul is careful. The investigation is conducted entirely outside formal Guild process, which means Cawl cannot use Guild resources openly.

Senna Vey contributes to the Salt-Ledger Circle's communal record, with particular attention to brine-sealed objects and the Tide Debts the Guild claims transfer to whoever takes possession of them. Vey is skeptical of the Guild's interpretation and documents cases where the transfer claim appears to be fabricated.

Vey and Tallow share information through the Salt-Ledger Circle's network, with Vey's systematic cataloguing complementing Tallow's firsthand proximity to Returning events. Together their records constitute the most complete parallel accounting of what the sea has been returning and when.

The Keepers of the Outer Lamp are the small group responsible for the lighthouse and its two beacons. The outer lamp's extinction — quiet, unannounced — has left the Keepers in a state of institutional paralysis, with the keeper offering no explanation and the Guild pressing for one.

The Keepers operate under the Guild's ritual and practical jurisdiction, as the lighthouse burns rendered tallow and its keeper is technically a Guild appointment. The keeper's unilateral decision to extinguish the outer lamp is an act of defiance the Guild does not know how to categorize.

The Salt-Ledger Circle's communal record-keeping is rooted in the Underpiers, where proximity to Returning events and the Estuary Hours has made parallel accounting a survival skill rather than a political act. The Circle's ledgers circulate through the district's trusted networks.

The Circle's salt-ledgers represent a rival system of memory-keeping that the Guild cannot control or subpoena. The Circle tracks Tide Debts and brine-sealed returns in ways that sometimes contradict the Guild's official Ledger of Absences, creating a documentary record of Guild overreach.

The Moors Compact exempts moor-folk from oil-tithe in exchange for stone maintenance. The Guild claims the original document is in the Ledger of Absences, which the moor-folk find deeply suspicious — they call the agreement 'the old bargain' and have their own understanding of its terms.

Vane's mandate covers three generations of unpaid harbor levies, which means examining Council records going back further than most current Councillors' tenure. The books show debts owed to persons who do not exist in any crown registry, which Vane is beginning to understand is not clerical error.

The audit's scope has expanded to include Guild financial records, since the Guild's oil-tithe system is intertwined with the harbor's commercial accounting. The Guild's insistence that oil-tithe is not a tax is the central legal dispute, and Vane has writs that could theoretically resolve it by force.

The Guildhall sits in the Pier District, at the social and commercial heart of the harbor town, where its presence is a constant reminder of the Guild's authority. The rendered-tallow lanterns outside the Guildhall burn brighter than any others in town.

The Saltgull Tavern is the Pier District's primary gathering place for informal conversation, where wicktenders drink after rounds and where news of Returning events circulates before reaching the Council or the Guild. The soft hour finds it empty but for the keeper.

The Guild's wicktenders frequent the Saltgull and report conversations of interest to senior lamplighters. The tavern keeper is aware of this and has developed a system of subtle signals to warn patrons when a wicktender is listening more carefully than usual.

Cawl conducts his most sensitive work from the Guildhall's inner sanctum, where the Ledger of Absences is kept. His investigation into the true-name leaks is conducted here, in the small hours before the soft hour, when he can be certain no wicktender is watching.

The Coldhaven Lighthouse stands on the bluff above the upper town, its seaward-facing outer lamp visible for miles when lit. Its position above the town means its extinction was visible to everyone, which is part of why the keeper's silence is so frightening.

The Breakwater and Saints' Walk extends from the harbor's edge, accessible from the Pier District. The Saints carved into the breakwater are oriented toward where the outer lamp should be burning, a detail that Sister Onella Drake finds increasingly significant.

The Hollow-Eyed's Niche is the carved recess housing one of the Breakwater Saints — the figure called the Hollow-Eyed — which is among the most visited and most heavily garlanded of the saints. The Guild lamp at its base has burned without interruption until recently.

The Pier Four Ruin is a collapsed structure in the Underpiers, already a site of loss before the surf-child appeared. During the Estuary Hours it floods completely, and residents report that the water around it smells more strongly of deep brine than elsewhere in the district.

The Standing Field is one of the moor-folk's maintained stone sites, deep enough in the Whistlepine Moors that harbor residents rarely visit. The stones' relationship to the fog is taken seriously by the moor-folk and dismissed as superstition by most Council members.

The Drove Road Crossing marks the boundary between the moors and the harbor town's hinterland, where moor-folk and harbor traders exchange goods under the Compact's protections. It is also where the fog behaves differently — thicker on the moor side, thinner toward the harbor.

The Drowning Reach is the stretch of water adjacent to the Underpiers where most Returning events originate. During the Estuary Hours, the boundary between the Reach and the district's flooded streets becomes indistinct, which is when things most often walk out of the water.

The child walked out of the surf from the Drowning Reach, appearing during the Estuary Hours when the boundary between water and district is most permeable. They have not aged, speak in dead dialect, and carry no record in any ledger — Guild or salt — prior to their return.

Mer Tallow's fish stall and residence are both in the Underpiers, making them a central node in the district's informal information network. Mer's proximity to the waterline means they have witnessed more Returning events than almost anyone else in town.

Roak's wicktender rounds include Joss Pell's walk-up, and the lantern-debt on Pell's household means Roak is required to note any irregularities in the household's light and report them to senior lamplighters. The relationship is professionally cordial and personally uncomfortable for both parties.

The Harbormaster's Residence occupies a position in the upper town that affords a view of the harbor and, on clear days, the lighthouse. Since the outer lamp went dark, Iselt Morrow has reportedly stopped looking in that direction.

The Customs House sits in the Pier District, where its records of harbor commerce are most relevant. The crown auditor's occupation of the building has made it a site of political tension, with Guild members and Council representatives both finding reasons to linger nearby.

Solen rents a room in an Underpiers tenement on a long-term arrangement, sleeping on a raised platform above the Estuary Hours' waterline. His landlord keeps a salt-ledger in the upstairs room and Vare has noticed without yet asking about it.

The Harbormaster's Council quietly commissioned Vare for a supplementary harbor survey after discovering their existing charts were two decades out of date. The coin is modest but steady; Harbormaster Morrow personally reviewed his initial draft and asked for a second pass on the Pier Four mudflats.

Iselt Morrow is Vare's principal client through the Council's supplementary survey. She has met with him three times in her private office, has asked careful questions about the Pier Four shoreline, and has paid him in coin from a purse rather than from Council funds on the last occasion — a detail he noted and has not raised.

Vare buys his daily fish at Mer Tallow's stall and has, by long Underpiers habit, drifted into the loose orbit of her counter. She has not invited him into anything; she has also not stopped him sketching the rafters above her chest, which he has done twice. He pays her in coin and once in a precisely measured plan of her stall's water-line, which she accepted without comment.

Lys Penharrow has hired Vare twice to chart the Tallowback's current after her groundings — she wants a working map of where the bottom has shifted since the outer lamp went dark. He delivered the first chart and is two-thirds through the second. Her account of what she saw on the bank's crest is one of the few things in his notes that he has not yet committed to ink.

Cawl has identified Caul as the most likely source of the true-name leaks but cannot move against them without proof. The investigation is conducted in secret because a public accusation that the Guild cannot substantiate would be more damaging than the leaks themselves.
The Tallowback is a shallow bank in the Drowning Reach, roughly two miles seaward of the breakwater. Boats avoid it by tradition; with the outer lamp dark, captains have begun grounding on it.
The Council Chambers sit at the foot of Pier Three in the Pier District, as stated in both the Pier District prose and the Chambers' own prose kernel.
The Inland Shrine stands at the inland end of the Upper Town's high street, tended by Sister Onella Drake. It is visited by both harbor residents and moor-folk.

The Wicktender's Hut is set into a granite recess halfway along the Saints' Walk on the harbor-facing side of the breakwater, used as a shelter and re-supply point during nightly lamp-lighting rounds.

Adwen Roak is the lighthouse keeper of Coldhaven, a hereditary post held by the Roak line for at least four generations. She is technically a Guild appointment but is not a wicktender — she is the lighthouse keeper and one of the three hereditary Keepers of the Outer Lamp.

Ifor Penny is the eldest stone-tender of the Standing Field on the Whistlepine Moors and effective authority among the moor-folk. She is not a leader of the Salt-Ledger Circle; the Circle is an Underpiers network she is connected to through Mer Tallow and the Moors Compact token.

Lys Penharrow is a fisher and captain working out of the Underpiers' lower landing. She is not a moor-folk representative; she is an Underpiers resident who carries a personal salt-ledger and has grounded twice on the Tallowback since the outer lamp went dark.

Brann Tew is a wicktender on the western Pier District route and serves Saints' Walk duty three nights in seven. He does not work at the lighthouse; his connection to the outer lamp is through his Saints' Walk duties and his observations passed to Joss Pell.

Brann Tew serves under the Lamplighters' Guild as a wicktender on the western Pier District route. He is not under the authority of the Keepers of the Outer Lamp, though his Saints' Walk duties have brought him into proximity with the lamp failures at the Hollow-Eyed's niche.
Brann Tew is a full wicktender of the Lamplighters' Guild, apprenticed at twelve and elevated at seventeen, currently walking the western Pier District route and Saints' Walk duty.

Joss Pell is one of the Salt-Ledger Circle's closest things to an elder, quietly reconstructing his old wicktender route's lantern-debts and passing observations to the network. The Circle prose explicitly names him alongside Mer Tallow.
Lys Penharrow carries a personal salt-ledger inside her shirt and is connected to the Circle's network through Mer Tallow, to whom she reported the figure she saw walking on the Tallowback.

Hesker Caul has been quietly visiting the Pier Four child once a fortnight since her arrival, taking down her speech in careful phonetic notation. He has not yet told Harbormaster Morrow what he has translated.

Adwen Roak is the lighthouse keeper of Coldhaven, third of her line in the post, responsible for both the inner and outer lamps. She extinguished the outer lamp at midsummer and has refused all Guild requests to inspect the housing since.

Adwen Roak is one of the three hereditary Keepers of the Outer Lamp, holding the lighthouse line's operative seal. Her unilateral extinguishing of the outer lamp is the act that has thrown the Keepers into crisis.

Ovin Cawl is the Guild line's hereditary Keeper of the Outer Lamp, having inherited the role on his father's death and opened the sealed letter that night. He has been in panicked private correspondence with Adwen Roak since the lamp went out.

Sister Onella Drake is the shrine line's hereditary Keeper of the Outer Lamp. She opened her letter ten years ago and has since stolen copies of the other Keepers' letters. She is the most informed of the three and the most carefully silent.

Mer Tallow and the Salt-Ledger Circle are sheltering the child who walked out of the surf. Tallow has been slowly recording the child's dead dialect speech in transliteration and has realized the child is naming people sold through the Naming Trade.

Mer Tallow has been recording the surf-child's dead dialect speech in transliteration. Ifor Penny, as the stone-tender who can read dead dialect, is connected to the child's significance through the far-listener lore, but it is Mer Tallow who directly documents the child's speech.

The Tallowback is the geometric center of Vare's unfinished problem. The Crestline Maren grounded there on the way in before breaking on the inner rocks; he has chartered passage on three fishing skiffs to take soundings, and the bearings he records do not match the bearings he took from the wreck. He has not told anyone the discrepancy exists.

The Pier Four ruin sits inside the Council's commissioned survey area, and Vare visits the mudflats at low tide to measure the surviving pilings. He has begun, without quite admitting it to himself, recording which names are chalked on the shrine's inner walls — and noticing that some appear in hands he has seen nowhere else in town.

Master Cawl received Vare formally once, over tea in the Guildhall's upper room, to ask after the survey's progress. The conversation was unfailingly courteous and Vare left it with the precise sense of having been measured himself. He has not returned the visit and has begun routing his Pier District work to avoid Guildhall sightlines.
